result: The study identified 45,050 TIPs using PopoolationTE2 with 97.1% sensitivity and 92.2% precision. Most TIPs are DNA transposons (84%), particularly MITEs from Stowaway (24%) and Tourist (20%) superfamilies, with 81.3% located within 5 kb of annotated genes.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41 provide comprehensive characterization of TIP detection methodology and results. The validation using MH63 genome (C35) demonstrates good performance metrics. The compositional analysis (C36-C39) and genomic distribution (C40-C41) are clearly stated with specific percentages, supported by the methods description.

result: TIP-eQTL mapping identified 563 significant associations in indica (477 genes, 3.1% of expressed genes) and 356 in japonica (317 genes, 2% of expressed genes). The proportion of TE orders in significant TIPs did not differ from genome-wide representation.
evaluation: Claims C42-C46 present the core eQTL mapping results with specific numbers and percentages. The statistical thresholds (MAF >3%, FDR <0.05) are clearly stated. Figure 1A-C provides visual support. The finding that TE order proportions don't differ significantly from genomic background (C46) is an important control observation.

result: TIPs explain more expression variance than SNPs for most genes with associated TIPs (~62% indica, ~73% japonica), uncovering genetic associations not observed with SNP markers alone.
evaluation: Claims C47-C48 and C155-C156 demonstrate the added value of TIP analysis over SNP-only approaches. Figure 1D provides visual evidence. The result was reproduced using combined SNP+TIP analysis and subsampled SNPs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), strengthening the conclusion. Specific percentages are provided.

result: TIPs more frequently have negative effects on gene expression (59%) compared to SNPs (53% negative), with variation among TE superfamilies (TIR/MULEs ~50%, LTR/Gypsy 67% negative). This suggests TIP-eQTLs are more frequently causal mutations.
evaluation: Claims C49-C54 analyze effect directionality with specific percentages. The inference that TIPs are more likely causal (C53) is supported by the directional bias and citation to comparable work in Capsella. The variation among TE types (C51-C52) adds mechanistic insight. However, the causal inference remains somewhat speculative without functional validation.

result: TIP-eQTLs are enriched in the 1 kb upstream region of genes (promoter regions), while SNP-eQTLs are more evenly distributed across genic regions, suggesting many TIP-eQTLs are causal mutations.
evaluation: Claims C55-C58 describe genomic location patterns supported by Figure 1E-F. The enrichment in upstream regions (C56) is a key observation supporting causality (C58). The interpretation is reasonable given that promoter elements typically reside upstream (C57), though linkage disequilibrium cannot be completely ruled out.

result: Low- and high-frequency TIPs (rare alleles) show the highest positive or negative effects on gene expression, consistent with the rare variant effect where deleterious mutations are maintained at lower frequencies.
evaluation: Claims C59-C62 describe the relationship between TIP frequency and effect size, supported by Figure 2A-D. The pattern is consistent with theoretical expectations (C59-C60) and the rare variant effect (C62). The citation to Lye et al., 2022 provides theoretical support. The U-shaped relationship in the figures is clear.

result: Most TIP-eQTLs (38.5% indica, 33.2% japonica at FDR threshold; 90% wet, 71% drought at relaxed threshold) are shared between wet and drought conditions with consistent effect directions, indicating general rather than stress-specific associations.
evaluation: Claims C63-C67 analyze condition-specificity with specific overlap percentages from Figure 2E-F. The high overlap when using relaxed thresholds (C64) strengthens the conclusion. The consistency of effect directions (C65) is important. The inference that most are general associations (C66) is well-supported, though the small number of stress-specific TIP-eQTLs (C67) is also noted.

result: Overlap between indica and japonica TIP-eQTLs is low (90 shared out of 919 total), with ~69% indica and ~60% japonica appearing subspecies-specific. Only 59 indica and 21 japonica TIP-eQTLs are truly subspecies-specific (completely absent in the other).
evaluation: Claims C75-C79 quantify subspecies-specificity with clear numbers from Figure 2E-F. The distinction between subspecies-specific at MAF >3% (C78) versus truly absent (C79) is important. All shared associations have consistent effect directions (C77). The low overlap contrasts with the high condition overlap, suggesting subspecies-specific regulatory evolution.

result: Among subspecies-specific TIPs, 56% indica-specific and 24% japonica-specific were present in wild rice (rufipogon/nivara), suggesting recent TE activity post-domestication. Some high-frequency subspecies-specific TIPs may be under positive selection.
evaluation: Claims C80-C84 analyze the evolutionary timing of TIPs. The presence in wild ancestors (C80-C81) is data-supported. The inference of recent TE activity (C82) is reasonable and supported by citations. The suggestion of positive selection for high-frequency insertions (C84) is plausible but requires the PBS analysis for confirmation.

result: 90% of TIP-eQTLs are present in both subspecies but at very different frequencies, suggesting they were present in the common ancestor and differentially retained. This pattern differs from non-eQTL TIPs, which show similar frequencies in both subspecies.
evaluation: Claims C85-C90 describe frequency patterns supported by Figure 2H-I. The contrast between eQTL-TIPs (different frequencies) and non-eQTL TIPs (similar frequencies) is a key observation (C89-C90). The inference of ancestral presence and differential retention (C88) is well-supported. This suggests selection on expression-altering variants.

result: 66% (552/829) of TIP-eQTLs are found in wild rice (rufipogon/nivara), confirming many are old insertions. Frequency differences between wild and cultivated rice may result from selection or genetic drift during domestication bottlenecks.
evaluation: Claims C91-C93 provide clear data on TIP presence in wild ancestors. The inference that these are old insertions (C92) is well-supported. The frequency differences (C93) are documented. However, the explanation for frequency changes (C94) is speculative, acknowledging both selection and drift as possibilities without distinguishing between them.

result: TIP-eQTLs show significantly higher PBS values than non-eQTL TIPs (mean 0.06 vs 0.02, p<0.01), with enrichment in extreme PBS values (>95th percentile, OR=4.87, p<0.01). 35% of TIP-eQTLs (119 genes) fall in the top 10% of PBS values, indicating positive selection.
evaluation: Claims C95-C99 present PBS analysis results with statistical support from Figure 3A. The Wilcoxon test (C95) and Fisher's exact test (C96) provide appropriate statistical evidence. The enrichment of TIP-eQTLs in extreme PBS values strongly supports the selection inference (C97, C99). The 35% figure (C98) quantifies the extent of selection.

result: Four MITE insertions (Tourist superfamily) are associated with EG2/OsJAZ1 expression. Three linked insertions (TIP_32891, TIP_32892, TIP_32894, r²=0.88) increase expression (Hap A), while one intronic insertion (TIP_32893) decreases expression (Hap B).
evaluation: Claims C102-C110 describe the EG2 locus with specific TIP identifications and effects. The linkage analysis (C106) supports the haplotype structure. The pangenome analysis (C108-C110) confirms two main haplotypes with opposite effects. Figure 4A-B provides visual support. This is a well-characterized example of TIP-mediated expression variation.

result: EG2 haplotypes show differential selection: Hap A (high expression) is at 48% in wild rice, increases to 65% in japonica (under positive selection with low π, high H12) but decreases to 16% in indica. Hap B (low expression) increases to 83% in indica (under selection), consistent with subspecies differences in spikelet number.
evaluation: Claims C111-C121 present comprehensive frequency and selection analysis for EG2 haplotypes. The frequency data (C111-C114) are clear. The selection statistics (C117-C120) from Figure 4C-F provide strong evidence for differential selection. The connection to spikelet phenotype (C115-C116, C121) is supported by citations, though the phenotypic link is correlative rather than directly demonstrated.

result: Two TIP-eQTLs affect OsGAP expression in japonica: TIP_50057 (upstream, increases expression, Hap A) and TIP_50059 (intronic, decreases expression, Hap B). Hap B frequency increases from 19% in wild rice to ~50% japonica and ~95% indica.
evaluation: Claims C122-C129 characterize the OsGAP locus with clear TIP locations and effects from Figure 5A-B. The haplotype structure (C127) and frequency changes (C128-C129) are well-documented. The functional annotation (C123-C124) is citation-supported. The near-fixation of Hap B in indica (C129) is a striking observation.

result: OsGAP Hap A (high expression) shows strong positive selection in japonica (low π, high H12) but not indica, despite Hap B near-fixation in indica. This suggests OsGAP-mediated dormancy control is relevant in japonica but not indica, consistent with different genetic regulation of dormancy between subspecies.
evaluation: Claims C130-C138 integrate functional information (C130-C133 from citations) with selection analysis (C135-C136 from Figure 5C-D). The subspecies-specific selection pattern is well-documented. The inference about dormancy relevance (C137) is reasonable but somewhat speculative. The citation supporting different dormancy regulation (C138) strengthens the interpretation.

result: TIP_45706 (LTR-RT upstream of OsMPH1) is associated with decreased expression and shorter plants. It increased from 11% in wild rice to 70% indica and 95% japonica, with strong selection in both subspecies, suggesting parallel selection for reduced plant height similar to SD1 during the Green Revolution.
evaluation: Claims C139-C148 present the OsMPH1 case with clear frequency data (C141), functional information (C142-C143), and selection evidence (C148 from Figure 6C-D). The parallel to SD1 (C144-C146) provides important context. The inference of parallel selection (C147) is well-supported by the frequency and selection data, though the actual phenotypic effect on plant height is inferred from prior work rather than directly measured.

result: 18% of genes with TIP-eQTLs have multiple TIPs associated with expression changes. Among genes with highest PBS values (strong selection), 43% have more than one TIP-eQTL, suggesting TIPs are important sources of expression variability in selected genes.
evaluation: Claims C159-C161 quantify TIP multiplicity at genes. The enrichment of multiple TIPs at highly selected genes (C160) is a key observation supporting the importance of TIPs in adaptive evolution (C161). The percentages are clearly stated. This pattern suggests TIPs cluster at functionally important loci.

result: Most TIP-eQTLs are old insertions present in wild ancestors (66% in rufipogon/nivara), highlighting the importance of standing variation for crop adaptation. Many have been positively or negatively selected in cultivated rice, translating into selectable phenotypic differences.
evaluation: Claims C162-C168 synthesize findings about TIP age and selection. The data on wild ancestor presence (C162) is well-supported. The comparison to tomato (C163) provides broader context. The inference about standing variation importance (C164) is reasonable. The selection evidence (C167) is supported by PBS analysis. The connection to phenotypes (C168) is inferred from selection patterns.

result: TE insertions are associated with expression changes in genes targeted during rice domestication and breeding, particularly signal transduction genes. These insertions were often present in wild ancestors and differentially selected in indica and japonica, with TEs serving as major drivers of selected expression variation.
evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C169-C170 represent the main conclusions synthesizing all results. The association with domestication/breeding genes (C2) is supported by specific examples (EG2, OsGAP, OsMPH1). The presence in wild ancestors (C3) and differential selection (C4) are well-documented. The focus on signal transduction genes (C5, C169) is supported by functional analysis. The conclusion about TEs as major drivers (C170) is justified by the comprehensive evidence.

result: The study used transcriptional data from 208 rice varieties (126 indica, 82 japonica) grown under wet and drought conditions to perform TIP-eQTL GWAS.
evaluation: Claims C28-C29, C32-C33 describe the study design and data sources. The use of Groen et al., 2020 data is clearly cited (C28). The methodology (C29) and sample composition (C32-C33) are explicitly stated. This provides the foundation for all subsequent analyses.

result: Specific TIP-eQTLs are associated with drought-related genes: TIP_49046 with reduced OsSYT-5 expression (drought tolerance when silenced), TIP_23764 with increased OsSAPK10 expression, and TIP_52367 with increased OsEULS2 expression.
evaluation: Claims C68-C74 provide specific examples of drought-related TIP-eQTLs. The associations are from the eQTL data. The functional information about these genes (C69-C71, C74) is citation-supported. These examples illustrate the biological relevance of TIP-eQTLs, though the actual drought phenotypes are not directly tested in this study.

result: Genes with TIP-eQTLs showing extreme PBS values are candidates for subspecies adaptation, including genes regulating plant architecture, development, and stress responses.
evaluation: Claims C100-C101 identify candidate genes for adaptation based on PBS analysis. This is a reasonable inference from the selection data (C100). The functional categories (C101) are supported by the specific examples presented (EG2, OsGAP, OsMPH1). This provides a framework for future functional studies.

result: TIPs may be more frequently causal mutations compared to SNPs, as suggested by their enrichment in upstream regulatory regions and greater variance explained.
evaluation: Claims C157-C158 synthesize evidence for TIP causality. The inference is supported by multiple lines of evidence: upstream enrichment (C56), variance explained (C47), and effect directionality (C50). However, this remains an inference without direct functional validation. The citations to comparable work (C157) provide additional support.

result: Background and context: TEs are major components of plant genomes and sources of genetic variability. TIPs have been shown to uncover additional phenotypic variance in GWAS studies. TEs can alter gene expression through various mechanisms including promoter interference, silencing, providing alternative promoters, and redistributing transcription factor binding sites.
evaluation: Claims C1, C6-C27 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims set the scientific context for the study but do not represent novel findings. They are well-supported by the cited literature and represent accurate summaries of prior knowledge about TEs, their mechanisms, and their role in crop evolution.

result: TIPs are frequently associated with changes in rice gene expression, and many TIPs altering regulatory gene expression have been positively selected in indica and japonica subspecies.
evaluation: Claims C30-C31 summarize the main findings. These are high-level conclusions supported by the detailed results (563 indica, 356 japonica TIP-eQTLs; PBS analysis showing selection). These claims effectively synthesize the key discoveries but are redundant with more detailed result claims.

result: Prior work has shown the importance of rare TE variants for gene expression variation in humans and plants, and structural variants including TIPs are linked to crop trait variation in tomato.
evaluation: Claims C149-C154 cite relevant prior work providing context for the current study. The citations to Goubert et al., 2020 (C149), Uzunović et al., 2019 (C150), and Alonge et al., 2020 (C153-C154) are appropriate. These claims establish the broader significance of the work but represent prior knowledge rather than novel findings.
